svg.title: The warrant is the soft spot
svg.desc: On the left, a diagram of the claim, evidence and warrant structure. At the bottom sits the evidence, the thing actually printed: children from lower-income households score lower on standardised tests. At the top sits the claim: cultural capital shapes educational outcomes. Between them, drawn as the link that carries the weight, sits the warrant: that the tests measure familiarity with dominant-class norms rather than innate ability. A marker shows that strengthen and weaken questions aim at the warrant, not at the data. A note explains that the warrant is usually unstated, so you have to supply it yourself: say out loud what would have to be true for this evidence to support this claim, and that sentence is what the answer choices will be attacking or shoring up. On the right, four disciplines with their level of analysis, their usual evidence and their characteristic move. Sociology works at the level of groups, institutions and structures, using surveys, census records, longitudinal studies and ethnography, and its characteristic move is to ask which theoretical tradition is speaking, functionalism, conflict theory or symbolic interactionism, since the same data serves all three. Economics works at the level of incentives, markets and allocation, using historical cases, policy analysis and experiments, and its characteristic move is to ask whether the rational-actor model is being used or being challenged. Psychology works at the level of the individual mind and behaviour, using experiments and replication debates, and its characteristic move is to watch the jump from a laboratory finding to a claim about the wider world, which is where its warrants hide. Anthropology works at the level of culture and cross-cultural comparison, using ethnographic fieldwork, and its characteristic move is to expect several descriptive paragraphs before the claim arrives, so ask what each description is supporting. A footer warns that scope is the other soft spot: evidence from three Pacific Island communities supports a claim about those communities, and an answer choice that quietly drops the qualifier is wrong however well it matches the theory.
svg.text: The warrant is the soft spot
